monitored_text: Fine-Tuning Tolerances for CNC Machined Parts Maximize part quality, reduce cost, and navigate design challenges using standardized tolerances on machined parts While tight tolerances are essential for certain features and assemblies, specifying greater precision than necessary can increase manufacturing costs, extend lead times, and complicate production. On the other hand, tolerances that are too loose can affect part fit and functionality. This guide covers standard CNC machining tolerances, geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T), and practical design considerations to help you achieve the required accuracy without unnecessary cost. Key Points Tolerances are important in assemblies, but apply them sparingly and only where function requires. In general, tighter tolerances increase manufacturing, measurement and quality assurance cost. Keep it simple. For the majority of components, ±1 mm is sufficient for noncritical features. In prototypes, adjust tolerances to validate what will be required in production. Use dimensionally stable materials where tight tolerance is important. Specify smoother surface finishes only where function requires them. Why Tighter Tolerances Aren't Always Better It is easy to apply tight tolerances and overconstrain features with geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GD&T) at the design and prototype stage. This will drive up manufacturing cost and limit sourcing options later in the development cycle. The most stringent tolerances may require secondary machining steps such as grinding, polishing or electrical discharge machining (EDM), increasing both cost and lead time. Likewise, tolerances that are too loose can make assembly difficult or impossible. To help navigate tolerance types and likely cost implications, this article covers tolerances available from Protolabs along with commonly used tolerances. We’ll also explore surface finish and GD&T (defined under BS 8888:2025 , ISO , and ASME Y14.5), and explain how tolerances are inspected. Standardized Tolerances for CNC Machining Standard tolerances vary by manufacturing route. The Protolabs automated factory holds ±0.005 in. (0.13 mm), while our semi-automated factory and the Protolabs Network follow ISO 2768-1 fine (f) for metals and medium (m) for plastics. Tighter tolerances are often achievable, so be sure to note any requirements on your design when you upload it. At Protolabs, our standard prototype and production machining tolerance is +/- 0.005 in. (0.13mm). But if you need greater accuracy, there's our standard precision or production machining tolerance of +/-0.002 in. (0.051 mm). We're also able to hold +/- 0.0005 in. (0.0127mm) on reamed holes, and +/- 0.002 (0.051mm) on feature locations, provided those features are machined on the same side of the part. Tolerancing Guidelines for CNC Machining Overconstraining a design can take two forms: adding an unnecessarily tight tolerance, or constraining each degree of freedom more than once. A single pin constrains x and y, while a second pin prevents rotation. The same applies to slots and inserts, and overconstraining will add cost. Tolerances can be bilateral (± 0.005 in), unilateral (+ 0.000/-0.010 in) or limit dimensions (1.005/0.995 in). All are acceptable, in imperial or metric units, provided they are stated clearly on the drawing. Surface Finish and Surface Roughness Surface roughness is referred to as Ra (roughness average). It is the mean of the peaks and valleys along a material’s surface, and is typically measured in micrometers (µm) or microinches (µin). Protolabs typically delivers a 1.6 µm (63 µin) Ra finish on flat and perpendicular surfaces across CNC machining materials. Curved surfaces are typically 3.2 µm (125 µin) Ra or better. For general CNC machining, Ra 6.3 µm to Ra 0.8 µm is typical. Optional bead blasting produces a slightly rougher but uniform matte finish that hides tool marks on cosmetic surfaces . See our surface finish guide for detailed images. Surface finish and tolerance are closely linked. A rough surface, for example, uses up part of a tight tolerance band. This means tightly toleranced features usually require smoother finishes. Anodizing, plating and powder coating add thickness, so be sure to factor that in on mating features (or be sure to mask critical surfaces). You should also be aware that each step down in Ra adds cost and lead time, so it’s a good idea to reserve smoother finishes for things like sealing faces, bearing surfaces, and sliding fits. Ra Comparison for CNC Machined Parts Ra (µm) Ra (µin) Surface appearance Typical applications Cost impact 3.2 125 Visible tool marks Non-critical and internal surfaces, brackets, housings Baseline 1.6 63 Slight tool marks General-purpose parts, light-load sliding fits Minimal 0.8 32 Faint tool marks, smooth to the touch Bearing surfaces, sealing faces, high-stress parts Moderate 0.4 16 Very smooth, near-reflective Pressure seals, high-speed rotating parts, medical components Highest; usually needs a finishing process Protolabs offers micro finishing for parts that need an Ra 0.4 µm finish. Designing In Adjustment Adding adjustment features helps achieve an accurate fit and test the tolerances required: Shimming: Use thin shim steel or shim washers to set height or close gaps. Adjustment screws: Set screws or fine pitch screws can alter position or push an assembly to a datum. Include a locking method such as a nylon-insert lock nut, thread locking compound or a secondary screw. Press fitting: Press two components to a known height or position. Shrink fitting: Heat the outer component so it expands enough to slide over the inner one. As it cools and contracts, it grips to form an interference fit. Another practical approach is to produce multiple design variants for assembly testing; CNC machining and 3D printing can quickly produce a test array. What Are Microns? The micrometer (µm) is one thousandth of a millimeter. When you hold your phone, the warmth of your hand can change its size by up to 68 µm. This puts our general tolerance of ±127 µm into context. Avoid measuring in microns unless parts are normalized for 24 hours and measured in a temperature-controlled environment using a CMM (which Protolabs offers). (Example: aluminum alloy CTE = 24 µm/m/°C; ambient 18 °C, body temperature 37 °C, phone length 150 mm.) Capability and Measurement Accuracy “Although Protolabs quoted ±0.1 mm on the aluminum parts, all dimensions were within ±0.05 mm.” Customer comment. Protolabs uses capability studies to maintain tolerance, so delivered parts often exceed the quoted tolerance, which covers multiple machining setups and material types. To achieve the best tolerance, follow this guidance: Where possible, orient interrelated features to be machined in one plane so they are produced in the same setup. Use materials with a low coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE). Specify plastics with low moisture absorption. Water uptake changes size and shape and can affect CNC machined glass-filled plastics. How Are CNC Tolerances Inspected? The right inspection method depends on the tolerance, the feature, and the type of documentation you require. Hand tools and gauges: Calipers, micrometers, height gauges, pin gauges and go/no-go thread gauges are fast and suit most standard tolerances. Coordinate measuring machines (CMMs): A CMM uses a touch probe to record points on a part and compare them with the CAD model or drawing. It measures the relationships GD&T describes, such as position, flatness, and perpendicularity, then produces a dimensional report. Optical and laser scanning: Non-contact systems capture whole surfaces quickly and suit complex profiles and delicate parts. Surface roughness testers: A profilometer draws a stylus across the surface to confirm the specified Ra. Upon request, we measure using CMMs (coordinate measuring machines), laser scanning and other metrology equipment. We also support the Production Part Approval Process (PPAP), provide a Certificate of Conformance (CoC) to your specifications, First Article Inspections (FAIs) and material data sheets. Geometric Dimensioning and Tolerancing GD&T gives designers a precise way to communicate critical manufacturing requirements to the manufacturer. It acts as concise notation; adding GD&T often specifies a sequence of manufacture and may imply a different process. Because it defines fit relationships between features, it increases the need for quality control, measurement and gauging. Common GD&T Symbols and Use Cases Characteristic Symbol Category Common use case Straightness ⏤ Form Shafts, pins, long edges Flatness ⏥ Form Sealing faces, mounting surfaces Circularity ○ Form Turned diameters, O-ring grooves Cylindricity ⌭ Form Bores and shafts that run in bearings Perpendicularity ⟂ Orientation Mounting faces, turned shoulders Parallelism ∥ Orientation Opposing faces, guide surfaces Angularity ∠ Orientation Angled faces and mounting features Position ⌖ Location Hole patterns, bolt circles, dowel holes Profile of a surface ⌓ Profile Complex contours and freeform surfaces Circular runout ⭧ Runout Turned diameters relative to an axis Total runout ⌰ Runout Shafts and other rotating parts Position tolerances often carry a maximum material condition (MMC) modifier, which allows “bonus” tolerance as a hole grows from its smallest size while still guaranteeing fit. ASME Y14.5-2018 removed concentricity and symmetry, but both remain in ISO 1101. You’ll need to check which standard your supplier works to. GD&T callouts require a 2D drawing alongside the 3D CAD model at upload. Limits and fits: Normally defined on a hole basis to ISO 286-2, limits and fits use a letter and number with the hole diameter. Holes use a capital letter (for example H7) and shafts use a lowercase letter (for example g6). The larger the number, the wider the tolerance band: 9 and above: typical milled or drilled tolerance 7: generally a reamed hole; a specific reaming tool is needed for each size 6 and below: requires more specialized machining The letter defines deviation from nominal. H is on nominal. k and higher are larger than nominal for an interference fit. g and lower are smaller than nominal for a clearance fit. True position: Usually specified as a diameter, which means the tolerance applies in every direction. A position tolerance of 0.030 diameter defines a cylindrical zone, so the hole’s axis can sit up to 0.015 from its true position in any direction. Reamed holes are typically required, as an irregular hole diameter will consume the GD&T allowance. Flatness: Milled surfaces are generally flat. Specifying very tight flatness usually implies surface grinding. Cylindricity, concentricity and runout: Runout is often specified because it is easier to measure. Runout is a compound measurement, so further checks may be needed to confirm cylindricity or concentricity. Squareness (perpendicularity and angularity): CNC milling machines are calibrated to ensure tools are square to the machine bed, which delivers good squareness, especially over short distances. FAQs What is the standard tolerance for CNC machining? expand_less expand_more At Protolabs, the standard machining tolerance is ± 0.005 in. (0.13 mm), with ± 0.002 in. (0.051 mm) available for precision work. This is sufficient for most noncritical features. What is a good surface roughness for CNC machined parts? expand_less expand_more Ra 1.6 µm (63 µin) suits most functional parts. Specify Ra 0.8 µm for bearing and sealing surfaces, and Ra 0.4 µm only where function demands it. Does a smoother surface finish mean tighter tolerances? expand_less expand_more Not automatically, but tight tolerances generally need a smoother finish, because surface peaks and valleys take up part of the tolerance band and make measurement less repeatable. When should I use GD&T instead of ± tolerances? expand_less expand_more Use GD&T when the relationship between features matters, such as hole patterns that must align with a mating part. For simple features, ± tolerances are quicker to specify and cheaper to inspect. Get a Quote We are here to support your project.
